verdict.rationale: At Pentecost the noun dialektos (G1258) in Acts 2:6 and 2:8 denotes a specific spoken language, with the relative clause en hei egennethemen (into which we were born) anchoring it to the mother tongue, and the ethnic catalogue of Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and Arabs makes the real-human-language reading lexically secure for that scene. The other noun glossa (G1100) is used interchangeably with dialektos in Acts 2:11, equating the two terms there. But in 1 Corinthians 14:2 the same glossa is paired with ouk anthropois lalei alla theoi (the speaker speaks not to men but to God), oudeis akouei (no one hears or understands), and mysteria lalei (he speaks mysteries), and 1 Cor 14:27 requires a diermeneutes (an interpreter, G1329) rather than a translator. 1 Cor 13:1 even contemplates glossais ton anthropon kai ton aggelon (tongues of men and of angels), extending the category beyond ordinary human speech. Because the proposition asserts one unified definition of the biblical gift while the lexical data splits into an immediately-intelligible-witness pattern in Acts and a needs-interpretation, directed-to-God pattern in 1 Corinthians, with the same lexeme bearing apparently different referents, the verdict is disputed: the Pentecost-bound clause is well supported, but the canon-wide identity claim is materially contested at the lexical level.

scripture.force: The disciples begin to speak heterais glossais (in other tongues) as the Spirit gave them apophthengesthai (to utter, declare). The adjective heterais marks the tongues as other than their own, and the immediately following narrative identifies those others as the native languages of the assembled nations.

Each one ekouon (kept hearing) the disciples lalounton (speaking) tei idiai dialektoi, in his own language. The noun dialektos here names a definite spoken human tongue, and the distributive idiai ties each hearer to his particular native speech, which fixes the Pentecost phenomenon as real-language communication received as intelligible.

The crowd asks how each akouomen (we hear) tei idiai dialektoi hemon en hei egennethemen, in our own language into which we were born. The relative clause en hei egennethemen anchors dialektos to the mother tongue of birth, which is the strongest lexical signal that Pentecost tongues were genuine ethnic languages, not non-cognitive utterance. The noun dialektos has six total NT occurrences (Acts 1:19, 2:6, 2:8, 21:40, 22:2, 26:14) and in every one denotes a real spoken human language, never ecstatic speech.

The hearers say akouomen lalounton auton tais hemeterais glossais (we hear them speaking in our own tongues) the megaleia tou theou (the great works of God). Here glossais is used interchangeably with dialektoi of verses 6 and 8, equating the two terms within the same pericope and confirming that the content was intelligible proclamation of God's deeds.

Paul writes ean tais glossais ton anthropon lalo kai ton aggelon (if I speak in the tongues of men and of angels). The coordinated genitive ton aggelon, joined to ton anthropon by kai, extends the category of glossa beyond ordinary human speech to a class denominated by angelic speakers. The construction is hypothetical (ean), so it does not by itself prove a non-human category is the Corinthian phenomenon, but it shows the Pauline use of glossa is not lexically restricted to ordinary human tongues.

The one lalon glossei ouk anthropois lalei alla theoi (speaking in a tongue speaks not to men but to God), oudeis gar akouei (for no one understands), pneumati de lalei mysteria (but by the spirit he speaks mysteries). Three lexical signals diverge sharply from the Acts 2 pattern: speech directed to God not to people, no human comprehension, and the content described as mysteria. At Pentecost the same root glossa is paired with immediate hearing in one's own dialektos, so this verse is the principal locus where the canon-wide identity of glossa fractures.

Paul says there are perhaps tosauta gene phonon (so many kinds of languages) in the world, kai ouden aphonon (and none without meaning or sound). The vocabulary of phone and aphonos shows Paul reasoning from the model of actual human languages, which is consistent with a real-language frame and supplies the analogy he then applies to the Corinthian gift.

If I do not know the dynamis tes phones (the force of the language), I will be barbaros (a foreigner) to the speaker and he barbaros to me. The noun barbaros is the technical term for one whose speech is an unintelligible foreign language, which both supports the real-language analogy and shows that in Corinth the tongue functioned as unintelligible to the hearer absent comprehension, a different effect from the immediate hearing at Pentecost.

If anyone lalei glossei (speaks in a tongue), let it be by two or at most three, kai ana meros (and in turn), and let one diermeneueto (interpret). The verb diermeneuo (G1329) is used here, not hermeneuo alone, the same compound that elsewhere renders Hebrew or Aramaic into Greek (compare Luke 24:27, Acts 9:36); its presence is compatible with both a translation and an explanatory rendering, but the requirement of such a mediator shows that in the Corinthian assembly the tongue was not automatically understood by hearers as at Pentecost.

If there is no diermeneutes (interpreter), let the speaker sigato (keep silent) in the assembly, and let him speak heautoi kai toi theoi (to himself and to God). The directed-to-God communicative aim, with the speech silenced in public when uninterpreted, contrasts with the public intelligible witness of Acts 2 and is the lexical crux that divides the readings.

Paul cites the Isaiah text en heteroglossois kai en cheilesin heteron laleso toi laoi toutoi (in other tongues and in lips of others I will speak to this people). The compound heteroglossos and the parallel cheilesin heteron describe foreign-language speech as a sign to unbelieving Israel, which leans the Corinthian gift toward real human languages and partially harmonizes it with Acts 2.

complicating_texts.resolution: The clause ho gar lalon glossei ouk anthropois lalei alla theoi (the one speaking in a tongue speaks not to men but to God) describes a communicative direction toward God rather than the human audience addressed at Pentecost, and the added clauses oudeis akouei (no one understands) and pneumati de lalei mysteria (he speaks mysteries in spirit) describe content that is opaque to hearers. The same noun glossa is used as in Acts 2, but the function differs: at Pentecost the speech is heard by men in their native dialektos as intelligible witness, while in Corinth the uninterpreted tongue is not understood by men. This is the principal reason the canon-wide identity of the gift is contested, so it is recorded as the driver of the disputed verdict rather than as a resolved harmonization.

Paul's statement that when he prays glossei his pneuma prays but his nous (mind) is akarpos (unfruitful) indicates that the speaker himself does not cognitively process the content. This is compatible with speaking a real but personally-unlearned language whose meaning the speaker does not consciously parse, yet it is also read by some as non-cognitive utterance, so the lexical data underdetermines the choice and the verdict remains disputed.

The phrase tais glossais ton anthropon kai ton aggelon (tongues of men and of angels) is hypothetical (ean) and rhetorical, so it does not by itself establish that the Corinthian gift includes angelic speech, but the very availability of the angelic category within the Pauline use of glossa shows the lexeme is not lexically restricted to ordinary human tongues. Whether the speaker meant a real but heavenly language or a non-translatable spiritual utterance is exactly what the words do not decide, which is why the proposition's universal claim is underdetermined.

variants.note: No CBGM-published variant units cover Acts 2 or 1 Corinthians 13 to 14 in scope. The minor apparatus markers visible in the bundle (for example the diairesis at apophthengesthai in Acts 2:4 and small readings in 1 Cor 14:10) do not alter the lexical sense of glossa, dialektos, mysterion, or diermeneuo, so the verdict holds across plausible variant readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Treats dialektos in Acts 2:6 and 2:8 as the controlling term, reads glossa in 1 Cor 14 as the same real-language gift heard as a foreign tongue, and points to barbaros (1 Cor 14:11) and the heteroglossos quotation of Isa 28:11 (1 Cor 14:21) as Pauline confirmation that the Corinthian phenomenon is foreign human language. Reads 14:2 lalei theoi as descriptive of the situation where no native speaker is present to hear, not as defining the gift's essence.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: two-phenomena (real in Acts, distinct in Corinth)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Holds that dialektos plus the named nations fix the Pentecost phenomenon as real human languages for intelligible witness, while 1 Cor 14:2 (lalei theoi, oudeis akouei, mysteria), 14:14 (nous akarpos), 14:27 to 28 (requires diermeneutes else silence), and the hypothetical aggelos in 13:1 describe a different gift directed to God whose content is opaque to hearers. On this reading glossa is polysemous across the two corpora and the proposition's unified definition is materially contested.

Treats glossa as non-translatable spiritual utterance even at Pentecost, reading dialektos as referring to the hearers' miracle of perception rather than the speakers' content (the miracle in the ear, not in the mouth). Cites lalei theoi, nous akarpos, mysteria, and tais glossais ton aggelon as defining the category, and reads Acts 2's catalogue of nations as a divine sign rather than a description of the speech itself.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on whether glossa in 1 Corinthians 13 to 14 is lexically identical to glossa equated with dialektos in Acts 2:6 to 2:11. The grammatico-historical data secures the Pentecost clause but leaves the canon-wide identity open, which is why three defensible lenses produce divergent verdicts. All three are recorded in their strongest lexical form so a reader holding any of them sees the position represented fairly.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What is the lexical referent of glossa and dialektos in the Pentecost narrative of Acts 2, and does that referent extend without remainder to glossa as used in 1 Corinthians 13 to 14?
stem_audit.notes: The proposition embeds a conclusion in three places: it asserts the gift is real human languages, asserts the languages are previously unknown to the speaker, and asserts the purpose is intelligible witness. The neutralized form asks the lexical question without presupposing the answer. The verdict was derived on the original stem; the audit confirms that the Pentecost portion is lexically supported while the universalizing claim that the same definition governs 1 Corinthians 14 is the contested element.

lay_summary: Two Greek words carry this question. In the Pentecost account in Acts 2 the crowd hears the disciples speaking and each one hears in his own dialektos, the noun for a specific spoken language or native dialect. Acts 2:8 anchors it tightly by adding into which we were born, and the listed nations, Parthians, Medes, Elamites, people from Egypt, Asia, Crete, and Arabia, show these were real ethnic languages. The content was the great works of God, heard and understood on the spot. Across all six times dialektos appears in the New Testament it always names a real spoken human language, never ecstatic speech. In Acts 2:11 the other word, glossa, is used as an equivalent. For that scene the words clearly point to genuine human languages spoken for intelligible witness. The difficulty comes when the same word glossa appears in 1 Corinthians. There Paul says the one speaking in a tongue speaks not to men but to God, that no one understands him, that he speaks mysteries by the spirit, and that his own mind is unfruitful. He also requires an interpreter, and if none is present the speaker must stay silent and speak only to himself and God. In 1 Corinthians 13:1 he even contemplates tongues of men and of angels. He does reach for foreign-language vocabulary, using the word barbaros for one whose speech you cannot understand, and quoting the prophet about other tongues, which leans toward real languages. But the directed-to-God aim, the no-one-understands, the mysteries, and the angels phrase pull the other way. So the words themselves strongly support the real-language and intelligible-witness reading for Pentecost, yet they do not settle whether the very same definition governs the Corinthian gift. Because the proposition asserts one unified definition across the whole canon, and the lexical evidence splits between an immediately understood pattern in Acts and a needs-interpretation pattern in 1 Corinthians, the overall picture is genuinely contested at the level of the words, rather than plainly established or plainly denied.
